Infra & Chips.content: # The AI chip money has quietly moved from training to inference ![Tarun Mishra](https://cdn1.wionews.com/prod/wion/author/images/2025/20250813/image-1755070388748.jpeg?imwidth=80&imheight=80) ![The AI chip money has quietly moved from training to inference](https://cdn1.wionews.com/prod/wion/images/2026/20260604/image-1780554095693.webp?rect=(0,156,936,702)&imwidth=600&imheight=450&format=webp&quality=medium "The AI chip money has quietly moved from training to inference") ## The AI chip money has quietly moved from training to inference ## Between January and August, twelve disclosed AI chip funding rounds raised $5.37 billion. Inference-focused companies took eight of those deals and roughly 67 per cent of the capital — a reversal from the years when training hardware attracted almost everything, and a signal about where investors think the durable spending lies. Between January and August, twelve disclosed AI chip funding rounds raised $5.37 billion. Inference-focused companies took eight of those deals and roughly 67 per cent of the capital — a reversal from the years when training hardware attracted almost everything, and a signal about where investors think the durable spending lies. Twelve disclosed AI chip funding rounds between January and August raised $5.37 billion. Inference-focused companies accounted for eight of the twelve deals and about 67 per cent of the capital. For most of the current AI cycle, the money and the attention went to training hardware — the chips used to build models. That is no longer where the majority of new chip capital is going. The Distinction, Briefly Training is the process of building a model: enormously compute-intensive, performed a limited number of times, dominated by a small number of organisations with the capital to attempt it. Inference is running the finished model to answer a query. Each individual operation is far cheaper, but it happens continuously, at whatever scale the product has users. Over a successful model's life, inference is where most of the compute is ultimately consumed. And so is an inevitable server upgrade cycle that has been a long time coming – and that has been delayed in part by AI spending and then accelerated as companies try to free up power and space in their datacenters by modernizing their application and database server fleets to make way for power-hungry AI servers. NEXTPLATFORM AD This is the opposite of the perfect storm, which is compounding bad news. As far as I know, we don’t have a name for that converse, so I guess we can just call it a harmonic resurgence. And now that the partners of Nvidia and AMD can make more GPU accelerators than they could several years ago, Dell is getting a lot more GPU allocations, and I think a disproportionately larger part of AI system orders because it has its supply chain and factories in order and can actually line up iron to run against its swelling GenAI revenue backlog. In a conference call going over the company’s second quarter of fiscal 2027 financial results, Jeff Clarke, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman, said that it took eight quarters to get 3,200 customers who had bought an “AI factory.” And the next 3,300 customers were closed in only three quarters, for a total of 6,500 unique organizations that have deployed AI systems with PowerEdge brands on them. A lot of those customers are Tier 2 clouds and service providers as well as neoclouds and sovereigns, but now large enterprises are also looking to Dell, their traditional server supplier, to not only upgrade their aging iron, but to supply AI clusters for inference and maybe some training as well. Dell’s server business is hitting on all cylinders, and Clarke explained that there were over 1.2 million servers in the Dell installed base that were at the PowerEdge 14G generation or older. The 14G machines were announced in 2017 and ramped in 2018. So this iron in on the order of eight years old or older. That is a long time to keep a server in the field, and the current 17G machines from two years ago and the forthcoming 18G machines due next month allow workloads to be consolidated massively. Clarke pegs it at anywhere from six to eight of these vintage servers collapsed to one 17G system, and anywhere from twelve to fourteen for one 18G machine. These are much more heavily configured 17G or 18G machines that customers are buying to do consolidations, and so they are inherently more expensive. Dell is also passing on increasing costs for DRAM, flash, CPUs, and other peripherals, which further boosts revenues for traditional servers. And so is an inevitable server upgrade cycle that has been a long time coming – and that has been delayed in part by AI spending and then accelerated as companies try to free up power and space in their datacenters by modernizing their application and database server fleets to make way for power-hungry AI servers. As far as I know, we don’t have a name for that converse, so I guess we can just call it a harmonic resurgence. And now that the partners of Nvidia and AMD can make more GPU accelerators than they could several years ago, Dell is getting a lot more GPU allocations, and I think a disproportionately larger part of AI system orders because it has its supply chain and factories in order and can actually line up iron to run against its swelling GenAI revenue backlog. In a conference call going over the company’s second quarter of fiscal 2027 financial results, Jeff Clarke, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman, said that it took eight quarters to get 3,200 customers who had bought an “AI factory.” And the next 3,300 customers were closed in only three quarters, for a total of 6,500 unique organizations that have deployed AI systems with PowerEdge brands on them. A lot of those customers are Tier 2 clouds and service providers as well as neoclouds and sovereigns, but now large enterprises are also looking to Dell, their traditional server supplier, to not only upgrade their aging iron, but to supply AI clusters for inference and maybe some training as well. Dell’s server business is hitting on all cylinders, and Clarke explained that there were over 1.2 million servers in the Dell installed base that were at the PowerEdge 14G generation or older. The 14G machines were announced in 2017 and ramped in 2018. So this iron in on the order of eight years old or older. That is a long time to keep a server in the field, and the current 17G machines from two years ago and the forthcoming 18G machines due next month allow workloads to be consolidated massively. Clarke pegs it at anywhere from six to eight of these vintage servers collapsed to one 17G system, and anywhere from twelve to fourteen for one 18G machine. These are much more heavily configured 17G or 18G machines that customers are buying to do consolidations, and so they are inherently more expensive. Dell is also passing on increasing costs for DRAM, flash, CPUs, and other peripherals, which further boosts revenues for traditional servers.
